page_title: Tripping over the potholes in too many libraries

sources.entry: Tripping over the potholes in too many libraries

summary.title: Tripping over the potholes in too many libraries
summary.one_liner: Learn the author's rule for when to avoid a third-party dependency: if you could write a replacement in an afternoon, write it yourself.
keywords: when to write your own library
takeaways: Adopting a dependency has hidden costs: searching, reading docs and code, and wiring it in can take hours.
Writing your own small tool gives you full knowledge of how it works and its shortcomings.
A custom solution can be shorter and faster because it solves only your specific problem.
Survey existing solutions first, then write your own using what you learned.
Software ecosystems tend to follow a cycle from good standard libraries to low-quality user libraries and DLL hell.
summary.summary: The author argues that some programming language ecosystems make it too easy to rely on poor-quality third-party libraries, and that broken dependencies can be hard to work around. The core rule is to never use a dependency that could be replaced with an afternoon of programming, since evaluating a library (searching, reading docs and code, wiring it up) takes hours anyway. The post notes that general libraries carry many bugs irrelevant to a specific use case, and it closes with a quoted tweet describing a recurring pattern in software ecosystems: a good standard library, then user libraries, then DLL hell, then low-quality libraries.
